22.title: The boy at the door
22.hook: Parvati makes a son from earth; sets him to guard her bath
22.howItsDone: Many Hindu families keep an image of Ganesha by the front door or at the entrance of a shop, as the guardian of thresholds, and his birth story is told to children and retold each year at Ganesh Chaturthi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita, the door to the whole mountain. Your line was you have the right to act. Not to the fruit. Camp 1 gave you twenty-one words. Camp 2 gives you stories. The first one starts in a bathroom. Day twenty-two.
screen: `YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO ACT. NOT TO THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Mount Kailash, home of Shiva and Parvati. And here is a very ordinary problem for a goddess: she wants to take a bath in peace. The door is guarded by Shiva's attendants, his ganas, loyal to him. Whenever Shiva wants to walk in, they step aside. Nobody in the whole house is simply hers. So one day, Parvati takes the paste she has rubbed on her skin before bathing, turmeric and oil and the dust of her own body, and she shapes it into a boy. Then she breathes life into him. He opens his eyes, and the first face he ever sees is his mother's. She hands him a staff and says: guard this door. Let no one in. No one at all. He nods. He has been alive for about four minutes. That boy grows up to be one of the most loved gods in India.
screen: `A GODDESS WANTS A BATH.` → `NOBODY IS HERS.` → `A BOY FROM EARTH.` → `GUARD THIS DOOR.`

segments.voice: You met Ganesha on day six, as a word. Now you get the story, and it's one that many Hindu children hear early. It's told in the Shiva Purana, one of the great old collections of stories about Shiva, and like most stories in this tradition it comes in more than one version. In this one, the boy is made from earth, from the stuff of his mother's own body. Not from a seed. Not from a sky god. From clay and turmeric, the ordinary stuff of a bath. People have loved that detail for centuries: the god of beginnings begins as dirt, shaped by hands. Here's what the story knows. Parvati doesn't make him because she's lonely. She makes him because she needs someone at the door. In a house full of loyal servants, all loyal to someone else, she wants one person whose whole job is to protect her space. Some things need a guard. A bath. A conversation. A quiet morning before the phone wakes up. And look at the boy. He is new. He knows nothing about who lives here or who outranks whom. He knows one instruction, and he means to keep it. That's why so many families hang a Ganesha by the front door. He's the keeper of thresholds, the one who stands where outside becomes inside. Tomorrow someone is going to walk up to that door, someone very large, who thinks it's his house too. And the boy is going to say no. For today, just hold the picture: a child made of earth, holding a staff, meaning every word.
screen: `MADE FROM EARTH AND TURMERIC.` · `SHE NEEDS SOMEONE AT THE DOOR.` · `NEW, AND ONE INSTRUCTION.` · `THE KEEPER OF THRESHOLDS.` · then, large: `SOME THINGS NEED A GUARD.`

segments.voice: This is your first two-minute sit. Here's the practice: guard your own door. Sit and breathe. Picture a door, the door to this quiet minute. Now notice what keeps knocking. A message you haven't answered. A worry about tomorrow. A replay of an argument. You don't have to fight them. Just stand at the door like the boy, and say, kindly: not now. Let them wait outside. Each time something knocks, notice it, and go back to guarding. Two minutes of a room that's just yours. The bell holds the time.
The boy at the door. Ganesha as a child, made by Parvati from earth, set to guard a threshold. The start of his story.
screen: `THE BOY AT THE DOOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: some things need a guard. Today, pick one small space, ten minutes, a meal, a walk, and guard it. No phone at the door. Day twenty-two.

23.title: Shiva comes home
23.hook: the fight; the head; Parvati's grief stops the universe
23.howItsDone: Hindus tell this story as part of Ganesha's birth, often at Ganesh Chaturthi; many hear in it both the seriousness of grief and Shiva's role as the one who destroys so that things can begin again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy at the door: Parvati's son, made from earth, with one instruction. Your line was some things need a guard. Did you guard ten minutes? Today, someone comes to the door. Day twenty-three.

Shiva has been away, meditating, the way Shiva does, for a very long time. He walks home up the mountain, to his own house, and at his own door there's a boy he has never seen, holding a staff. The boy says: you can't come in. Shiva says: this is my house. The boy says: my mother said no one. Anyone. Shiva sends his ganas to move the child. The boy beats them back. More come. He beats them back too. The gods arrive to help, and in the Shiva Purana even they can't get past him. This is a house fight that has turned into a war. And then Shiva, who has never been told no at his own door, raises his trident. And the boy's head is gone.
screen: `A STRANGER AT HIS OWN DOOR.` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.` → `THE TRIDENT.`

segments.voice: Stop there for a second, because this is a hard story, and the tradition doesn't soften it. Both of them are right. The boy is keeping his word to his mother. Shiva is trying to walk into his own home. Nobody is the villain, and something terrible happens anyway. Most family fights look like that. Now Parvati comes out. And her grief is not quiet. In the Shiva Purana, she is so angry and so heartbroken that she calls up goddesses, fierce forms of her own power, and sends them to swallow the universe. Heaven starts to come apart. The gods who fought the boy now come begging. The sage Narada and the gods plead with her, and she gives them her terms: bring my son back to life, and give him a place of honor among you. Otherwise, no universe. Here's what the story knows. First: grief has power. This tradition doesn't tell a mother to calm down. Her grief is so big that it stops everything, and everyone has to deal with it. Second: the one who broke it has to fix it. Shiva, the great god, the destroyer of worlds in his own story, now has to mend what he broke. And he agrees. That's the turn. What broke can be mended. Not unbroken. The boy will not come back the same, and tomorrow you'll see how he comes back. But mended. For Hindus, Shiva is the god who destroys so things can begin again. Here, he gets to learn that from the inside.
screen: `BOTH OF THEM ARE RIGHT.` · `HER GRIEF STOPS THE UNIVERSE.` · `THE ONE WHO BROKE IT MENDS IT.` · then, large: `WHAT BROKE CAN BE MENDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a broken thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something in your life that broke. A friendship. A promise. Maybe something you broke yourself, without meaning to. Don't try to fix it right now. Just look at it honestly, the way Parvati refused to pretend. Then ask one question: is there a way this could be mended? Not made new. Mended. If you pray, you can hold it up to God. If you don't, just hold it. The bell holds the time.
Shiva comes home. The fight at the door, the trident, and Parvati's grief, strong enough that the gods agree to mend what they broke.
Your line: what broke can be mended. Today, take one small step toward mending something: a text, an apology, a glue bottle. Day twenty-three.

24.title: The elephant facing north
24.hook: the search; the head; the boy lives
24.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin weddings, housewarmings, new ventures and other ceremonies by honoring Ganesha first, often with a short prayer or mantra to him before anything else begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shiva came home, and a boy lost his head at the door. Your line was what broke can be mended. Today, the mending. Day twenty-four.

Shiva gives an order to his ganas: go north. Bring back the head of the first living creature you meet. So they run, down off the mountain, into the forests, heading north. And the first creature they find is an elephant. In the version most families tell, it's lying asleep with its head toward the north. They bring the head back. Shiva sets it on the boy's body, and breathes life into him, and the boy opens his eyes, for the second time in his life. His mother is there again. But now he has a trunk, and wide ears, and a face every child in India can draw by the age of four.
screen: `GO NORTH.` → `THE FIRST CREATURE YOU MEET.` → `AN ELEPHANT.` → `HE OPENS HIS EYES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: People ask, fairly: why an elephant? The story's plain answer is: it was the first creature they met. But Hindus have been finding meaning in that face for a long time. Big ears, to listen more than he speaks. A small mouth. A trunk that can uproot a tree or pick up a single grain of rice. An elephant doesn't go around the forest. It walks through, and makes a path. That's why Ganesha is called the remover of obstacles. You met that on day six. Now you know where the face came from. The versions differ, and it's worth saying so. The Shiva Purana tells it as you heard it: north, the first creature. Popular tellings add the sleeping elephant with its head to the north. Another text, the Brahmavaivarta Purana, tells a different story, where the head is lost for another reason entirely. The tradition keeps them side by side. Here's the part that matters most. When the boy wakes, Shiva doesn't just forgive him. He honors him. He makes him the leader of the ganas, the very guards who fought him. That's his name: Ganesha, Ganapati, lord of the ganas. And Shiva makes a promise, with all the gods listening: this boy will be worshipped first. Before any other god. Before any ceremony. So to this day, a Hindu wedding, a housewarming, a new business, a first day of school, often starts with Ganesha. First, before anyone. The boy who was killed at the door becomes the one who opens every door.
screen: `WHY AN ELEPHANT?` · `BIG EARS, A PATH THROUGH.` · `THE VERSIONS DIFFER.` · `WORSHIPPED FIRST, BEFORE ANY GOD.` · then, large: `FIRST, BEFORE ANYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gratitude for a mend in your life. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that broke, and came back different, but whole. A friendship after a fight. A body after an injury. You, after a hard year. Maybe it came back with a new face, like the boy. Just thank it, or thank whoever helped mend it. If you pray, you can say thank you to God. The bell holds the time.
The elephant facing north. The first creature found, whose head brought the boy back to life, and a promise: he'll be honored first.
Your line: first, before anyone. Today, begin one thing well: before the first email, the first bite, the first word, pause for one breath. Day twenty-four.

25.title: The race around the world
25.hook: Ganesha vs Kartikeya: one circles the earth, one circles his parents
25.howItsDone: Hindus walk pradakshina, a clockwise circle keeping the holy on their right, around temple shrines, sacred trees and the wedding fire; this story is often told to children to explain why parents are honored.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elephant facing north, and Shiva's promise. Your line was first, before anyone. Did you pause before something began? Today, Ganesha gets a brother, and a race. Day twenty-five.

Two brothers. Kartikeya, the warrior, fast and bright, who rides a peacock. And Ganesha, round and patient, who rides a mouse. Their parents, Shiva and Parvati, set a contest. Whoever goes around the whole world first, wins. Kartikeya doesn't even wait for the end of the sentence. He's on his peacock and gone, over mountains, over oceans, around the entire earth. Ganesha looks at his mouse. The mouse looks at Ganesha. There is no way this ends well. So Ganesha stands up, walks over to his mother and father, and slowly, carefully, walks in a circle around them. Then he bows. And he says: I'm done.
screen: `A PEACOCK AND A MOUSE.` → `AROUND THE WHOLE WORLD.` → `HE CIRCLES HIS PARENTS.`

segments.voice: Kartikeya lands, out of breath, and finds his brother already declared the winner. And Ganesha explains. In the Shiva Purana's telling, he says the scriptures teach that walking around your parents with devotion is the same as walking around the whole earth. My world is right here. I just went around it. Here's what the story knows. The walk is a real thing. It's called pradakshina: circling something holy, keeping it on your right. Hindus do it at temples, around a shrine, around a sacred tree, around the fire at a wedding. It says: this is the center, and I move around it. So Ganesha isn't pulling a trick. He's doing exactly what people do at every temple in India. He's just saying where his center is. Now, the versions. In the Shiva Purana, the prize is who gets married first, and Ganesha does. In the telling loved across South India, the prize is a single fruit, a fruit of wisdom, brought by the sage Narada. When Kartikeya, called Murugan there, loses, he leaves home and goes to live on a hill, and that hill, Palani in Tamil Nadu, is one of his great temples today. Millions climb it. So the story has two winners, depending on who tells it. And that's worth holding. Kartikeya isn't the fool. He actually went around the world. Ganesha just noticed that the world he cared about was a few steps away. The whole world is close.
screen: `MY WORLD IS RIGHT HERE.` · `PRADAKSHINA — CIRCLING THE CENTER.` · `A WEDDING, OR A FRUIT.` · `KARTIKEYA ISN'T THE FOOL.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD IS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk a slow circle. If you can, stand up. Pick a center: a chair, a plant, a photo of someone you love. Walk slowly around it, keeping it on your right, the way people circle a shrine. One step per breath. As you walk, think of the few people who are your whole world. If you can't walk right now, trace a slow circle with one finger, around their names. The bell holds the time.
The race around the world. Kartikeya circles the earth. Ganesha circles his parents, and says his world is right there.
screen: `THE RACE AROUND THE WORLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the whole world is close. Today, go around your world once: call, text or sit with one person who is the center of it. Day twenty-five.

26.title: The broken tusk
26.hook: the pen breaks mid-Mahabharata; he snaps his tusk to finish
26.howItsDone: Ganesha is honored as a patron of writing and learning; many Hindus write his name or the syllable Om at the top of a new notebook, account book or manuscript before they begin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the race around the world, and Ganesha circling his parents. Your line was the whole world is close. Who did you go around? Today, look closely at his face. One tusk is missing. Day twenty-six.

Look at almost any image of Ganesha and count the tusks. One. The other is snapped short, and often he's holding the broken piece in his hand. There's a story for that, and it's a writer's story. The sage Vyasa has the longest poem in the world in his head, the Mahabharata. He needs someone to write it down as he speaks. He asks Ganesha. Ganesha says yes, on one condition: once I start, you can't stop. If you pause, I leave. Vyasa says fine, on one condition of my own: you can't write a single line until you understand it. And they begin. Days of it. Then, somewhere in the middle, Ganesha's pen breaks.
screen: `COUNT THE TUSKS.` → `THE LONGEST POEM.` → `DON'T STOP. UNDERSTAND.` → `THE PEN BREAKS.`

segments.voice: He can't stop. That was his own rule. So, the story goes, he snaps off his own tusk, dips it in the ink, and keeps writing. That's why he's called Ekadanta: the one with one tusk. Now, honesty about sources, because this tradition cares about them. The scribe story, Vyasa dictating and Ganesha writing, appears at the beginning of the Mahabharata in many old manuscripts. But the scholars who built the modern critical edition left that passage out, because many of the oldest manuscripts don't have it. And the tusk as a pen is a later telling still; other Puranas explain the broken tusk in different ways, including a fight with the warrior-sage Parashurama. The tradition keeps all of them. So hold the story as a story people love, not a record. And look at what it knows. First: the two conditions. Ganesha says, don't stop. Vyasa says, understand before you write. Tradition says Vyasa slipped in knotty verses to slow his scribe down and get a breath. Speed and understanding, keeping each other honest. Second: the tool breaks, and the work doesn't. Ganesha gives up something of his own, something permanent, so the work gets finished. He's the remover of obstacles, and in this story the obstacle is a broken pen, and the answer is himself. Everyone has a half-finished thing. A letter. A course. A drawer. The story doesn't say it'll be easy. It says finish the thing, even if it costs you a tusk.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish one small unfinished thing. Sit and breathe first. Let one unfinished thing come to mind, something small enough to finish today. An email half-written. A dish in the sink. A thank-you you never sent. Picture yourself finishing it, start to end. Notice what's been stopping you. When the bell rings, if you can, go and finish it. The bell holds the time.
The broken tusk. Ganesha as Ekadanta, the one-tusked, who in the story snapped his tusk to keep writing the Mahabharata.
Your line: finish the thing. Today, one small unfinished thing gets its last line, even if it costs you a little. Day twenty-six.

27.title: The mouse
27.hook: a mountain of a god rides a mouse
27.howItsDone: In Hindu temples and home shrines a god's vahana often sits facing the deity; at Ganesh Chaturthi Ganesha's mouse is placed at his feet, sometimes with its own small offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the broken tusk, and a pen that couldn't stop. Your line was finish the thing. Did something get its last line? Today, look down, at Ganesha's feet. Day twenty-seven.

Here's a picture that makes children laugh. Ganesha: big belly, elephant head, four arms, sitting like a king. And under him, carrying the whole thing, a mouse. A tiny mouse, often looking up at him, sometimes nibbling a sweet. It makes no physical sense at all, and that's the point. In this tradition, almost every god has an animal that carries them. Shiva rides Nandi, the bull. Vishnu rides Garuda, the great eagle. Durga rides a lion. Saraswati has her swan. Kartikeya, from the race, has his peacock. And the god of beginnings, the remover of obstacles, rides the smallest of them all. Today's word is the name for that animal.
screen: `A BIG GOD. A TINY MOUSE.` → `EVERY GOD HAS A RIDE.` → `THE SMALLEST OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Vahana. From a Sanskrit root, vah, to carry. A vahana is the one that carries: a vehicle, a mount. And a god's vahana isn't just transport. It tells you something about the god. The bull is strength and patience, the eagle is speed, the lion is courage. So why a mouse? Hindus give more than one answer, and it's worth hearing a few. One: a mouse gets into everything. Through walls, under doors, into the grain store. It finds a way in where nothing bigger could. That's what the remover of obstacles does. Two: the mouse is desire, restless, nibbling at everything, never satisfied. Ganesha sits on it. Not killing it. Riding it. Steering it. Wanting doesn't go away; it just stops being in charge. Three, and simplest: the huge is carried by the small. There are stories, too, about where the mouse came from. In some Puranas it's a being who was cursed, or a demon Ganesha defeated who became his mount. Those stories vary a lot, and no single one is the official answer. What almost everyone shares is the picture. At Ganesh Chaturthi, the mouse sits at his feet in millions of homes and street shrines, often with its own little offering. And here's the thing a curious person could say tonight. That mouse is doing the heaviest lifting in the whole image. Small carries large. Every day. Quietly. Nobody writes songs about it.
screen: `VAHANA — THE ONE THAT CARRIES.` · `THE MOUNT SAYS WHO THE GOD IS.` · `IN EVERYWHERE, OR DESIRE RIDDEN.` · `THE STORIES VARY.` · then, large: `SMALL CARRIES LARGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one small thing carrying something big. Sit and breathe. Look around you, or think back over today. What small thing is holding up something large? The chair under you. One bolt in a bridge. The person at the front desk. A single habit that keeps your week from falling apart. Pick one. Just look at it, and give it credit. The bell holds the time.
Vahana. The one that carries: the animal each god rides. Ganesha's is a mouse.
Your line: small carries large. Today, thank one small thing, or one quiet person, that carries a lot. Day twenty-seven.

28.title: Modak
28.hook: why he's always eating; the sweet as a gift that returns
28.howItsDone: At temples and home shrines Hindus offer food to the deity and then share it as prasad; at Ganesh Chaturthi many families make modaks, offer them to Ganesha, and give them out to family and neighbors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vahana, and the mouse that carries a god. Your line was small carries large. Today closes Ganesha's week, with the thing that's always in his hand. Day twenty-eight.

Look at his hand. Not the one holding the tusk. The other one, usually low, near that round belly. It's holding a sweet. A modak: a little dumpling of rice flour, pinched shut at the top like a flower bud, filled with coconut and jaggery. Ganesha is famous for loving them. One of his names means the one who loves modaks. At his festival, Ganesh Chaturthi, families make them by the trayful, and many make twenty-one at a time. There's a story people tell about his appetite. A rich god, Kubera, proud of his wealth, invites Ganesha to a feast to show off. Ganesha eats everything. Every dish. Every pot. And he's still hungry. Nothing Kubera owns can fill him.
screen: `A SWEET IN HIS HAND.` → `THE ONE WHO LOVES MODAKS.` → `A FEAST THAT CAN'T FILL HIM.`

segments.voice: In the telling, what finally satisfies him is something tiny: a handful of plain food, given with love. Not the feast. The love. The story isn't found in one fixed text; it's the kind families pass down. But what it points at is at the heart of how Hindus pray with food. Today's word: prasad. It means grace, a gift given freely. Here's how it works. At a temple or a home shrine, food is offered to the god. Sweets, fruit, rice. It sits before the image for a while. Then it's taken back and shared with everyone there. And now it's different. It isn't leftovers. It's prasad: the same food, returned as a blessing. You receive it with your right hand, often both hands cupped, and you don't waste a crumb. So the offering comes back. You give, and what you gave is handed back to you, and you share it. That's why Ganesha is always eating. It isn't greed. He's the one who receives first, so that everyone else can receive after. Now look back at the week. A boy made of earth, guarding a door. A trident, and a mother's grief. An elephant's head, and a promise: first, before anyone. A race, and a small circle around the people who are your world. A broken tusk, and the thing finished. A mouse, carrying a mountain. And a sweet, handed back. Seven days with one god. Tomorrow, a monkey who tried to eat the sun.
screen: `A HANDFUL, GIVEN WITH LOVE.` · `PRASAD — GRACE, GIVEN FREELY.` · `OFFERED, THEN HANDED BACK.` · `A WEEK WITH GANESHA.` · then, large: `THE OFFERING COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share food with someone. Right now, sit and breathe, and think about who you'll eat with next. Picture handing them something: a piece of fruit, half your snack, a cup of tea. Notice how it feels to give it before you eat. If you pray, you can offer your next meal to God before you eat it. If you don't, just offer it to the person across from you. Then, after the bell, actually do it. The bell holds the time.
Prasad. Grace: food offered to God and handed back as a blessing, to be shared.
Your line: the offering comes back. Today, share one thing you'd have eaten alone, and notice what comes back. Day twenty-eight.

fork.setup: you're Kubera. you've fed Ganesha every dish in your palace, and he's still hungry. what do you do?
options: cook even more, bigger, richer.
ask for help, and see him fed with a small handful given with love.
tell him the feast is over.
fork.reveal: in the telling, the feast fails and the small gift given with love satisfies him. a story families pass down, not one fixed text.

original.note: Sanskrit: grace, favor, clearness; the food handed back after an offering.

trapdoor: what you thought: a god with a sweet tooth.
what it means: the offering is received first, then handed back as prasad to be shared.
what a scholar hears: prasada in older Sanskrit also means clarity and calm of mind; the gift and the grace are the same word.

sources.ref: popular Ganesha tradition (Kubera's feast; Ganesha as lover of modaks)
